title: Real-world use cases of AI agents
notes: Agents already do real work in customer support, coding, research and operations, usually with a person checking what matters.
A good first agent job is repetitive, needs lookups to answer, and has mistakes that are easy to spot and cheap to fix.
Start with one narrow job and add the next only when the last one works reliably; that is how Scout grows in this course.

slides.title: Real-world use cases of AI agents
slides.sub: Where agents earn their keep today, and how to spot a good first job for one
sentences: You know what an agent is, and when a simpler system would do the job better.
Now let's look at where agents are actually used, outside of demos.
Then you will learn three questions that tell you whether a job is a good first agent project.

slides.title: Where agents work today

cards.title: Customer support
flow: Answers, or hands to a person

cards.title: Coding
flow: A change for a developer to review

sentences: Agents are already doing real work, and three areas stand out.
In customer support, an agent reads a question, looks up the order or account, and answers, or hands over to a person.
In coding, an agent reads files, edits code and runs the tests again, and a developer reviews the change.
In research, an agent searches the web, reads what it finds and writes a summary with its sources.
Notice what they share: each makes several lookups, and each decides what to look at next.
And in every one of them, a person still checks the result that matters.

slides.title: Operations: the delayed tents
slides.scenario: A supplier emails Orbit: the next batch of green Trailhead tents will arrive two weeks late.

steps.text: The supplier's email arrives in Orbit's inbox
The agent finds every open order waiting for that tent
It drafts a short, personal note to each of those customers
Leo reads the drafts and sends them with one click

result.text: Customers hear the news from Orbit before they have to ask, and a person approves every message.

sentences: The fourth area is operations: the behind-the-scenes work that keeps a business running.
Picture this at Orbit.
A supplier emails to say the next batch of green tents will arrive two weeks late.
An agent reads the email and finds every open order that is waiting for that tent.
For each one, it drafts a short note to the customer, explaining the delay.
Leo reads the drafts and sends them with one click.
Customers hear the news before they have to ask, and a person still approves every message that goes out.

slides.title: What agents do well, and where they struggle

left.label: Good at
points: Working at any hour, at scale

sentences: Before we pick a first job, let's be honest about strengths and weaknesses.
Agents are good at understanding messy requests written in plain language.
They are good at choosing which lookup to make next, and at drafting replies and summaries.
And they work at any hour, on hundreds of requests at once.
But they struggle with facts they have no way to look up, and they can fill the gap with a confident guess.
Long tasks with many steps give more chances for one step to go wrong.
And judgement calls with real money or safety at stake still belong with people.

slides.title: Three signs of a good first agent job
slides.lead: Before you build anything, check the job against three questions.

bullets.text: Repetitive: it comes up many times a week, each time a bit different
Needs lookups: the answer lives in a system, not in the question
Recoverable: a mistake is easy to spot and cheap to fix

aside.label: If it fails the test
aside.text: A person, a help page or a simple workflow probably does the job better.

sentences: So how do you choose a good first job for an agent?
First, it is repetitive: it comes up many times a week, and each time it is a little different.
Second, it needs lookups: the answer lives in a system, like an orders database, not in the question itself.
Third, mistakes are recoverable: if the agent gets one wrong, someone can spot it and fix it cheaply.
A job that fails these checks is usually better done by a person, a help page or a simple workflow.

slides.title: Checking Orbit's jobs

note.text: Only the order question passes all three, which is why Scout starts there.

sentences: Let's run four of Orbit's jobs through those three questions.
Where is my order passes easily: it comes up hundreds of times, needs a lookup, and a mistake is easy to correct.
Do you sell gift cards repeats a lot, but the answer is the same for everyone, so a help page is enough.
Approving a three hundred and ten dollar refund needs lookups, but once the money is sent, a mistake is hard to undo.
And choosing next year's suppliers is rare and high stakes, which makes it a job for people.
Only the order question passes all three, which is exactly why Scout starts there.

slides.title: Start narrow, then grow

note.text: Add one job at a time, and only when the last one works reliably.

sentences: One last lesson from real projects: start narrow.
Scout's first job is order status, and nothing else.
Once that works, it learns to answer policy questions about returns and shipping.
Then it handles exchanges, checking the stock before it offers a new size.
Only later does it touch refunds, and big ones always wait for a person.
Each new job is added only when the last one works reliably, and that is the path this course follows.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: Agents already work in support, coding, research and operations
Good first jobs repeat often, need lookups and forgive mistakes
Rare, high-stakes or irreversible decisions stay with people
Start with one narrow job, then grow

sentences: Let's recap.
Agents already do real work in support, coding, research and operations.
A good first agent job repeats often, needs lookups, and has mistakes that are cheap to fix.
Rare, high stakes or irreversible decisions stay with people, or at least wait for their approval.
And start with one narrow job, then grow.
Next, we open Scout up and look at the four parts every agent is built from.

midQuiz.q: In the delayed-tents example, what does Leo still do?
options: Nothing: the agent sends every note by itself
He reads the drafted notes and sends them
He writes every note by hand
midQuiz.explain: The agent does the searching and the drafting; Leo approves what goes out. A person still checks the result that matters.
midQuiz.hint: Look at the last step before the result.

midQuiz.q: Which is one of the three signs of a good first agent job?
options: It happens rarely, but each case is very important
The answer lives in a system and needs a lookup
Mistakes can't be undone, so speed matters most
midQuiz.explain: Good first jobs are repetitive, need lookups, and have mistakes that are easy to fix. Rare, high-stakes or irreversible jobs are poor first choices.
midQuiz.hint: Think about where the answer to "where is my order?" actually lives.

endQuiz.q: Which Orbit job is the best first job for an agent?
options: Approving refunds over $200 on its own
endQuiz.explain: Order questions repeat hundreds of times, need a lookup, and mistakes are easy to correct. Big refunds and supplier choices are rare, costly or hard to undo.
endQuiz.hint: Run each one through the three questions: repetitive, needs lookups, recoverable.

endQuiz.q: Why does Scout start with order status and add refunds much later?
options: Start narrow: add a job when the last one works, and keep risky actions for later
endQuiz.explain: Each job is added once the last one works reliably, and actions that move money come last, with a person approving the big ones.
endQuiz.hint: Think about which actions are easy to undo, and which aren't.
